e.etymology: From the English word serenity, calm or peacefulness, from Latin serenus, clear and calm. In general use as a name since the 1990s.

assoc.t: Serenity Prayer, used in twelve-step programs
Serenity, the spaceship of Firefly and its 2005 film

e.etymology: A pet form of Josephine, the French feminine of Joseph, Hebrew for he will add. Now often given as a full name.

assoc.t: Josie and the Pussycats, Archie Comics band and cartoon

e.etymology: From the English word legend, a celebrated story or person, from Latin legenda, things to be read. A 21st-century American word name.

assoc.t: legend, a famous story or a celebrated person
John Legend, singer and songwriter (stage surname)

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English ac, oak, plus leah, woodland clearing: a clearing in an oak forest.
namesakes: Annie Oakley (sharpshooter of Buffalo Bill's Wild West show)

assoc.t: Oakley, sunglasses and sports eyewear brand
Annie Oakley, Wild West sharpshooter

e.etymology: From the surname of the Protestant reformer John Calvin, a Latinized form of French Cauvin, a nickname for a bald man, from Latin calvus, bald.

assoc.t: Calvin, the boy in the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes
Calvin Klein, fashion and underwear brand

e.etymology: From an English surname, a variant of Payton, taken from place names usually explained as the settlement (tun) of a man named Pæga. Quarterback Peyton Manning made it a household name.
namesakes: Peyton Manning (Hall of Fame NFL quarterback)

assoc.t: Peyton Manning, Hall of Fame NFL quarterback
Peyton Place, 1956 novel and TV soap of small-town scandal

e.etymology: A pet form of Mildred, Millicent, Emily, Amelia and Camilla, long used as a full name as well.
namesakes: Millie Bobby Brown (actress, Eleven in Stranger Things)

assoc.t: Thoroughly Modern Millie, 1967 film and Broadway musical

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English cyninges tun, the king's town or manor. Many places bear the name, including the capital of Jamaica.

assoc.t: Kingston, capital of Jamaica
Kingston, computer memory and flash drive maker

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Charles, from Latin Carolus, which goes back to Germanic karl, free man. It keeps the -s of the Latin nominative, unusual in Spanish.
From Greek Iason, linked to iaomai, I heal. In myth Jason led the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece; a Jason also appears in the New Testament.
namesakes: Jason Bourne (amnesiac spy of the Bourne films)

assoc.t: Jason Voorhees, masked killer of Friday the 13th
Jason, leader of the Argonauts in Greek myth

e.etymology: A 20th-century American combination of Rae and Lynn, part of the wave of girls' names ending in -lyn.
A modern spelling of Riley, from an English place name, Old English ryge, rye, plus leah, clearing, or from the Irish surname Reilly.
From French Rémi, the name of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, traditionally derived from Latin remex, oarsman. A boys' name in France, it is given mostly to girls in the US.

assoc.t: Remy, rat chef of Pixar's Ratatouille (spelled Remy)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of John, from Old Spanish Johan and Latin Iohannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, Yahweh is gracious. Juan is also the Manx form of John.
namesakes: Juan Ponce de León (Spanish explorer of Florida)

assoc.t: Don Juan, the legendary seducer
Juan Valdez, mascot of Colombian coffee

e.etymology: The English form of Irish Ruairí and Scottish Gaelic Ruairidh, from Old Irish Ruaidrí, red king. Gilmore Girls, whose Rory is short for Lorelai, helped make it a girls' name in the US.
namesakes: Rory Gilmore (the bookish daughter on Gilmore Girls)

assoc.t: Rory Gilmore of Gilmore Girls
Rory McIlroy, golf champion

e.etymology: The feminine of the Roman name Lucius, from Latin lux, light. Saint Lucia (Lucy) of Syracuse, a Sicilian martyr, is honored with candlelit processions in Scandinavia each December.

assoc.t: Saint Lucia, Caribbean island nation

e.meaning: valley; or dean, a church or college official
e.etymology: From an English surname with several sources, chiefly Middle English dene, valley, and the title dean, a church official, from Latin decanus, leader of ten.
namesakes: James Dean (star of Rebel Without a Cause)
Dean Martin (Rat Pack singer and actor)

assoc.t: dean, a college or church official
James Dean, 1950s film icon (surname)

e.etymology: A short form of Judas, used to tell the apostle Judas Thaddaeus, Saint Jude, apart from Judas Iscariot. It goes back to Hebrew Yehudah (Judah), traditionally read as praised.

assoc.t: Hey Jude, the Beatles' 1968 hit
St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

e.note: In German, Jude is the ordinary word for Jew, which can make the name awkward with German speakers.

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a Middle English nickname for a hunter, from Old French chacier, to hunt. It is also the ordinary word chase.

assoc.t: Chase, the JPMorgan Chase consumer bank
Chase, the police pup in PAW Patrol

e.etymology: The Latin form of Eve, from Greek Eua and Hebrew Chavah, traditionally linked to the Hebrew word for life. In Genesis she is the first woman.
namesakes: Eva Perón (Evita, first lady of Argentina)

e.etymology: Heaven spelled backward. It took off after rock singer Sonny Sandoval of P.O.D. gave the name to his baby daughter in 2000.
e.note: Widely recognized as heaven spelled backward; often misspelled (Neveah) and mispronounced.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Malakhi, my messenger or my angel. Malachi is the last of the twelve minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible.
From Greek Leon and the word leon, lion, the source of Latin Leo. Also used as a short form of Leonard and Leonardo.

assoc.t: Kings of Leon, rock band
Léon, the hitman of the 1994 film The Professional

e.meaning: juniper, an evergreen with aromatic berries
e.etymology: From the juniper tree, a word English took from Latin juniperus. As an older surname it was sometimes a form of Jennifer. A 21st-century favorite among nature names.

assoc.t: juniper, the evergreen whose berries flavor gin

e.etymology: From an English surname, most often a nickname from Old English col, coal or coal-black, and sometimes a medieval short form of Nicholas.

assoc.t: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme
Cole, the earth ninja in LEGO Ninjago
Cole Haan shoes and Kenneth Cole fashion brand

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English hæth, heath, plus leah, woodland clearing.
The Italian form of Matthew, from Latin Matthaeus and Greek Matthaios, from Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of the Lord.
A short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. Long used as an independent name, it was especially popular in the 19th century.
namesakes: Eliza Doolittle (the flower girl of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady)
Eliza Hamilton (wife of Alexander Hamilton and a lead of the musical Hamilton)

assoc.t: Eliza Doolittle of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady
ELIZA, the pioneering 1960s chatbot
Eliza Hamilton, Alexander's wife in the musical Hamilton

e.etymology: Of uncertain origin. Edmund Spenser used Arlo as the name of a hill in The Faerie Queene, probably adapting the Irish place name Aherlow. Folk singer Arlo Guthrie made it familiar as a first name.
namesakes: Arlo (the young dinosaur in Pixar's The Good Dinosaur)

assoc.t: Arlo, home security camera brand
Arlo, the dinosaur of Pixar's The Good Dinosaur

e.etymology: From an English surname meaning son of Daw, a medieval pet form of David.
namesakes: Jack Dawson (Leonardo DiCaprio's character in Titanic)
Dawson Leery (the lead of Dawson's Creek)

assoc.t: Dawson's Creek, late-1990s teen TV drama

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English æsc, ash tree, plus tun, settlement.

assoc.t: Ashton Kutcher, actor

e.meaning: of the Roman Julius family; perhaps youthful
e.etymology: The feminine of Julius, the Roman family name of Julius Caesar, whose origin is uncertain; it is traditionally explained as youthful or downy-bearded. Early Christian saints spread the name.
